sections.section_title: The Corinthian Slogan and Paul's Response
sections.summary: Paul engages a Corinthian slogan -- 'it is good for a man not to touch a woman' -- signaling a shift to questions the Corinthians raised in their letter, and prepares to qualify and correct the absolutist ascetic position.

sections.section_title: Marriage, Mutual Obligation, and the Body
sections.summary: Paul counsels that because of the danger of sexual immorality each person should have their own spouse, establishes remarkably symmetrical mutual obligations between husband and wife regarding conjugal rights and bodily authority, and permits only temporary, mutually agreed abstinence for prayer.

Paul clarifies that his counsel on marriage is a concession rather than a command, expresses his personal wish that all were celibate as he is, but acknowledges that each person has their own charisma from God -- some for celibacy, some for marriage.
Paul counsels the unmarried and widows that remaining single is good, but those who cannot exercise self-control should marry, since it is better to marry than to burn with unfulfilled desire.

Paul relays the Lord's own command that a wife should not separate from her husband and a husband should not divorce his wife, with the qualification that if separation occurs, the wife should remain unmarried or be reconciled.

sections.section_title: Mixed Marriages -- Believers Married to Unbelievers
sections.summary: Paul gives his own counsel for marriages between believers and unbelievers: if the unbeliever consents to stay, the believer should not divorce, because the unbelieving spouse is sanctified through the believing partner; but if the unbeliever departs, the believer is not enslaved, since God has called them to peace.

sections.section_title: The Principle of Remaining -- Called, Circumcised, Enslaved
sections.summary: Paul articulates the chapter's governing principle -- each person should remain in the condition in which God called them -- and illustrates it with circumcision and slavery, arguing that neither external status needs to change because what matters is keeping God's commandments, and all believers were bought with a price.

sections.section_title: Concerning the Unmarried and the Present Distress
sections.summary: Paul offers his own judgment that in view of the present distress it is good to remain as one is, counseling against seeking marriage or divorce while explicitly affirming that marriage is not sin, though it will bring worldly troubles he would spare them.

sections.section_title: The Shortened Time and the Passing Form of the World
sections.summary: Paul grounds his practical counsel in eschatological urgency: the appointed time has grown short and the present form of this world is passing away, so believers should hold all earthly arrangements -- marriage, mourning, rejoicing, possessions -- with a loose grip.

Paul explains his preference for celibacy by describing how marriage necessarily divides attention between the Lord and the spouse, while the unmarried person can devote themselves wholly to the Lord, though he states this for their benefit and not as a restraint.

Paul addresses the specific case of a man betrothed to a virgin, affirming that marrying is not sin and the one who marries does well, while the one who refrains does even better in the present circumstances.
Paul states that a wife is bound to her husband as long as he lives but is free to remarry after his death -- only in the Lord -- though in his judgment she is more blessed if she remains as she is.
